issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only after independently reviewing the record and finding that the trial court's view was perverse or unreasonable and caused a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after disbelieving three eyewitnesses, while the High Court reappreciated the eyewitness, medical, and forensic evidence and convicted the surviving accused.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitnesses’ accounts consistent in material respects and found no tangible matter in cross-examination that impaired their credibility.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to interfere because the trial court erred in rejecting the eyewitness testimony; the Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s reversal of the acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court may reappreciate the evidence and reach an independent conclusion, but must consider the material on record and the trial court’s reasons and interfere only if the acquittal rests on a perverse or unreasonable view resulting in a miscarriage of justice. If two views are possible, the appellate court should not substitute its view for the acquittal. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for this principle here.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and (trial_view_perverse or trial_view_unreasonable) and miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_perverse: The trial court’s assessment of the evidence is perverse.
predicates.trial_view_unreasonable: The trial court’s assessment of the evidence is unreasonable.
predicates.miscarriage_of_justice: The trial court’s view results in a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When an acquittal is appealed, interference is justified if the trial court’s view is perverse or unreasonable and results in a miscarriage of justice.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to a victim does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony when the witness’s presence is natural and the testimony is credible and corroborated.
material_facts: The principal eyewitness was the son of one deceased person and the nephew of another; the injured eyewitness was the brother of two deceased persons; and another eyewitness shared land interests with the victims.
The eyewitnesses corroborated one another on material aspects, and lengthy cross-examination did not impair their credibility.
One eyewitness was injured in the incident, and the Supreme Court found no reason to doubt his presence or testimony.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationships to the deceased did not justify rejecting their testimony; the High Court was justified in relying on it.
issues.legal_principle: There is no legal bar to examining family members or other persons known to the affected party. Related or friendly witnesses’ testimony cannot be discarded merely because of their relationship if their presence is natural and their credible, reliable testimony is corroborated. An injured witness’s evidence stands on a higher pedestal. The Court relied on Mano Dutt and Another v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2012) 4 SCC 79, and Dayal Singh and Others v. State of Uttaranchal, 2012 (7) Scale 165.

rule.if: criminal_case and witness_is_related and witness_presence_natural and testimony_credible and testimony_corroborated

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of a person for a criminal offence.
predicates.witness_is_related: A witness is related to a victim or is otherwise known to the affected party.
predicates.witness_presence_natural: The witness’s presence at the place of the incident is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.testimony_credible: The witness’s testimony is credible and remains unimpaired after cross-examination.
predicates.testimony_corroborated: Other evidence or witnesses corroborate the witness’s testimony.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, relationship alone does not justify rejecting a witness’s testimony when the witness was naturally present and the credible testimony is corroborated.

issues.legal_issue: The death of co-accused after conviction does not, by itself, entitle a surviving accused convicted for participation in a group crime to exoneration.
material_facts: The High Court convicted the appellant and two other accused of group offences arising from a shooting in which five people died and one person was injured.
The two other convicted accused died while the appeal was pending, leaving the appellant as the sole surviving appellant.
The Supreme Court found clinching evidence of the appellant’s participation in the shooting.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not be exonerated merely because the other convicted accused had died; the conviction was not disturbed on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The appellant had been convicted under Sections 148, 307 and 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. In light of the evidence establishing his participation, the death of the co-accused did not itself justify exonerating him.

predicates.appeal_from_group_offence_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for offences involving participation in a group crime.
predicates.co_accused_died_after_conviction: Other convicted accused died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.evidence_establishes_surviving_accused_p: The evidence establishes the surviving accused’s participation in the crime.

issues.definition: A surviving accused appealing a group-offence conviction is not exonerated merely because co-accused die after conviction when the evidence establishes the surviving accused’s participation.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in disposing of a criminal appeal does not, by itself, require the accused to be discharged or exonerated.
material_facts: The State’s appeal against acquittal remained pending in the High Court for about twenty-five years before it was decided.
The appellant sought exoneration on the ground of that delay.
The case concerned five deaths and one injured person.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not be exonerated merely because the High Court took about twenty-five years to dispose of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply to criminal proceedings unless an express and specific provision makes it applicable. A criminal offence is a wrong against the State and society as well as against an individual. The Court relied on Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak, (1992) 1 SCC 225; Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, (1994) 3 SCC 569; P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka, (2002) 4 SCC 578; and Ranjan Dwivedi v. C.B.I., through the Director General, decided on 17 August 2012.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a criminal case.
predicates.prolonged_appellate_delay: The appeal has taken a prolonged time to be decided.
predicates.exoneration_sought_only_for_delay: The accused seeks discharge or exoneration on the ground of delay alone.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, prolonged appellate delay alone does not require exoneration when delay is the sole ground relied upon.
